name: The Implementation Citadel
description: Network implementation — routing, switching, wireless, and physical infrastructure.

nodes.name: Pathfinding
nodes.description: Routing protocols, admin distance, NAT, and first-hop redundancy.

encounters.title: The Logistics of Routing: The GlobalRoute Express
encounters.scenario: You're the Logistics Director for GlobalRoute Express, moving packages across a vast highway network. Every local sorting hub has a DEFAULT GATEWAY — its single exit point for any destination not known locally. If a driver has a package for an unfamiliar city, they don't wander side streets; they head straight to the hub, which routes it onward. Without this gateway, the driver is stuck in a loop with no way out. Two other concepts matter for routing decisions: STATIC ROUTING is a printed instruction sheet ('take Highway 5') — reliable but unchanging even if Highway 5 closes. DYNAMIC ROUTING is a GPS that constantly shares real-time road-closure data and recalculates automatically. ADMINISTRATIVE DISTANCE is a trustworthiness score — if two sources give conflicting directions, the router trusts the one with the LOWER AD.
encounters.question: A local delivery driver has a package for a city they have never heard of. To ensure the package leaves their local area and enters the wider network, where must they go first?
encounters.explanation: The Default Gateway is the local network's 'exit point' — when a device doesn't recognize a destination as local, it forwards the packet here to be routed onward toward the wider network. Without it, traffic to unknown destinations has nowhere to go.

encounters.title: The Grand Hotel Gateway
encounters.scenario: You're standing in the lobby of the 'Network Grand Hotel' — a huge building with hundreds of guest rooms, but only ONE official street address: 100 Connectivity Lane. This is the hotel's PUBLIC IP — to the outside world, the whole hotel is just one entity at that address. Inside, every guest has a room number (Room 302, Room 505) — these are PRIVATE IPs, useful for finding each other inside, but meaningless to an outside mail carrier who has no idea which hotel 'Room 302' belongs to. The FRONT DESK — the NAT (Network Address Translation) device — solves this: when a guest sends mail, the clerk swaps 'Room 302' for the hotel's public address. When a reply arrives, the clerk checks the logbook and delivers it to the right room. If hundreds of guests share one phone line, each gets a unique 'extension number' for outgoing calls — this is PAT (Port Address Translation).
encounters.question: A delivery driver has a package for 'Room 202,' but they don't know which building in the city it belongs to. Which networking concept acts like the building's front desk?
encounters.explanation: Just as a front desk uses the building's main address to route mail to specific rooms, NAT uses a single public IP to route traffic to multiple private IP addresses inside the network.

encounters.question: Which routing protocol has an administrative distance of 110?
encounters.explanation: OSPF has AD 110. EIGRP = 90, RIP = 120, eBGP = 20. Lower AD = more trustworthy route.

encounters.question: A directly connected route has an administrative distance of:
encounters.explanation: Directly connected routes have AD 0 — the most trusted source. Static routes are AD 1, eBGP is 20, EIGRP is 90.

encounters.question: Which type of NAT maps many private IP addresses to a single public IP using port numbers?
encounters.explanation: PAT (Port Address Translation) / NAT Overload maps many internal IPs to one public IP by tracking unique port numbers. This is what home routers do.

encounters.question: Which FHRP protocol is an open standard (non-Cisco proprietary)?
encounters.explanation: VRRP (Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol) is an open RFC standard (RFC 5798). HSRP and GLBP are Cisco proprietary. PVST+ is Cisco's per-VLAN spanning tree.

encounters.question: A network admin wants a static route to only be used if the OSPF route fails. What technique achieves this?
options: Set the static route metric to 255
Configure a floating static route with AD higher than 110
Disable the static route by default
encounters.explanation: A 'floating static route' has its AD set higher than the dynamic protocol (e.g., AD 150 > OSPF AD 110). The static route only appears in the routing table when the OSPF route is gone — making it a backup path.

encounters.title: The Gatekeeper's Map of Trust
encounters.scenario:
You approach the Great Crossroads where two paths lead toward the Citadel. A stone sentinel blocks your path, holding a weathered scroll. 'To pass,' the sentinel booms, 'you must decide which map is most trustworthy when the paths overlap.'

The sentinel explains that in this realm, routers use Administrative Distance (AD) to determine the reliability of a route source. A lower AD means the router trusts that source more. He shows you a table of common values:
- Directly Connected: 0
- Static: 1
- EIGRP Internal: 90
- OSPF: 110
- IS-IS: 115
- RIP: 120
- EIGRP External: 170
- BGP: 200
encounters.question: A router receives two different paths to the same destination network: one advertised via OSPF and another via RIP. Which path will the router choose as its primary route?
encounters.explanation: The router chooses the path with the lower Administrative Distance (AD). Since OSPF has an AD of 110 and RIP has an AD of 120, OSPF is considered more trustworthy.

encounters.title: The Shield of the First Hop
encounters.scenario:
You reach a bridge guarded by two massive stone golems acting as gateways. A nearby scroll explains that these golems work together to provide a 'Virtual Gateway.' This ensures that if one golem falls, the travelers can still cross without interruption.

This concept is known as First Hop Redundancy Protocols (FHRP). They create a Virtual IP (VIP) that serves as the default gateway for hosts. The scroll lists three specific types: HSRP (a Cisco-proprietary protocol), VRRP (an open standard used by many vendors), and GLBP, which specifically allows for load-balancing across multiple gateways.
encounters.question: Which of the following protocols is an open standard that provides first hop redundancy?
encounters.explanation: VRRP (Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol) is the industry-standard open protocol. HSRP is Cisco-proprietary, and GLBP is also a Cisco-proprietary protocol that adds load balancing.

encounters.title: The Shadow Path
encounters.scenario:
You find a hidden path leading through the Whispering Woods. A mystic tells you that this is a 'Floating Static Route.' It is a clever trick used by mages to create backup paths for travelers.

A floating static route works by assigning it an Administrative Distance higher than the primary route. For example, if your main road has an AD of 1 and your secret path has an AD of 100, the router will ignore the secret path as long as the main road is clear. Only when the main road collapses does the 'floating' route rise to take its place.
encounters.question: You configure a floating static route with an AD of 150 to serve as a backup for a primary static route with an AD of 1. When will the router use the backup route?
options: Only when network traffic exceeds a certain threshold
Always, because it is a valid static route
Only if the primary route becomes unavailable
Never, because its AD is too high
encounters.explanation: A floating static route stays 'hidden' (inactive) because its higher AD makes it less preferred than the primary route. It only enters the routing table if the primary route fails.

encounters.title: The Realms of the Great Web
encounters.scenario:
You stand before a massive map showing the interconnected kingdoms of the digital world. A scholar explains that there are two types of realms: Internal and External.

Interior Gateway Protocols (IGP) like OSPF and EIGRP are used to share information within a single organization or 'Autonomous System.' Exterior Gateway Protocols (EGP) are used to pass information between different organizations. The most prominent EGP is BGP, the protocol that stitches together the various networks of the internet, allowing data to travel across the globe.
encounters.question: Which of the following is an example of an Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) used to route traffic between different Autonomous Systems?
encounters.explanation: BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is the standard EGP used to route data between different Autonomous Systems on the internet. OSPF, EIGRP, and IS-IS are all IGPs used for internal routing.

encounters.title: The Weaver of the Weave
encounters.scenario:
You stand before the Great Gateway of Aetheria, where the flow of data is governed by the ancient laws of the Weaver. The Weaver, a spectral entity composed of shimmering fiber-optic threads, blocks your path. 'To pass,' she intones, 'you must prove you can discern the most specific path through the tangled web of the realm.'

A caravan of packets destined for the sacred coordinates 10.0.0.50 is stalled at the gate. The Weaver presents three scrolls of navigation: one from the OSPF Order (a broad path to 10.0.0.0/8), one from the EIGRP Guild (a more focused path to 10.0.0.0/16), and a Forbidden Scroll—a static route carved in stone for the precise destination of 10.0.0.0/24.

The Weaver's eyes glow with a piercing light as she demands you determine which scroll the Gatekeepers will honor to guide the packets home. She warns that many novices are fooled by the 'authority' of the scrolls, failing to see the truth of the path's specificity.
encounters.question: A packet destined for 10.0.0.50 arrives at a router. The routing table contains three entries: 10.0.0.0/8 via OSPF (AD 110), 10.0.0.0/16 via EIGRP internal (AD 90), and 10.0.0.0/24 via a Static route (AD 1). Which path will the router select?
options: The OSPF route, because it is the first entry in the routing table.
The EIGRP route, because it has a lower Administrative Distance than OSPF.
The Static route, because Longest Prefix Match takes precedence over Administrative Distance.
No path will be chosen because there are multiple routes for the same destination.
encounters.explanation: In routing logic, the 'Longest Prefix Match' is the first criteria used to determine the best path. A /24 mask is more specific than a /16 or a /8 mask. Administrative Distance (AD) is only used as a tie-breaker when two different routes have the exact same prefix length. Because 10.0.0.0/24 is the most specific match for the destination 10.0.0.50, it is chosen regardless of the AD values of the other competing routes.

nodes.name: The Switchboard
nodes.description: VLANs, 802.1Q trunking, Spanning Tree, and link aggregation.

encounters.title: The Office Building: Understanding VLANs
encounters.scenario: Picture a multi-story office building owned by one company. The third floor belongs to Finance, the fifth to Marketing — and they must stay separate; a Marketing intern shouldn't access Finance's payroll files. This separation is a VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) — invisible walls within the building. Even though Finance and Marketing share the same physical elevator (the switch), they operate in completely isolated logical spaces — a message from Finance reaches only Finance. Why bother? BROADCAST DOMAINS. If one computer shouts 'Who is the printer?', on a flat single network EVERY device hears and processes it — noise and congestion. Segmenting into VLANs shrinks broadcast domains: now only Finance devices hear Finance's question. This cuts congestion and improves performance while keeping departments isolated.
encounters.question: In a coffee shop, one customer asks 'Who has the Wi-Fi password?' loudly. If everyone in the shop hears this question and must process it, what networking concept is this demonstrating?
options: A broadcast within a broadcast domain
encounters.explanation: A broadcast domain is the area of a network where a broadcast frame is heard by all devices. VLANs break large broadcast domains into smaller, more manageable segments.

encounters.title: The Mailroom Logic: MACs and Switching
encounters.scenario: You're the new Lead Mail Clerk at 'The Ethernet Apartments.' Every resident has a unique, permanent nameplate on their mailbox — their MAC ADDRESS. Unlike a room number (an IP address), which can change if a tenant moves, the MAC address is hard-coded into the device and never changes. When Alice hands you a letter for Bob, you check your CAM TABLE (logbook) — but Bob isn't listed yet. So you BROADCAST: stand in the lobby and announce 'Bob, identify your location!' Everyone hears it, but only Bob responds. You record 'Bob = Apt 4B' in your logbook — the switch has LEARNED. Next time, no shouting needed: you check the logbook and UNICAST directly to his door. Unlisted residents still require a broadcast.
encounters.question: If an IP address is like your current mailing address (which changes if you move), what is a MAC address most similar to?
encounters.explanation: A MAC address is a permanent, unique identifier assigned to the hardware, much like a Social Security Number, whereas an IP address is a logical address that can change.

encounters.title: The Highway Loop Prevention Authority
encounters.scenario: You're the lead traffic engineer for Aetheria, designing the highway system. One thing you must prevent: THE INFINITE LOOP. If three highway interchanges connect in a triangle with no exit ramps, a confused driver circles forever — in networking, this is a BROADCAST STORM, packets circling endlessly and consuming all bandwidth. SPANNING TREE PROTOCOL (STP) prevents this: it doesn't tear down roads, it puts up 'Road Closed' signs at strategic points so there's exactly ONE logical path between any two points. First, an authority elects a 'Central Command Center' (the ROOT BRIDGE) — all decisions flow from there. Each ramp is then either 'Active' (FORWARDING) or 'Closed but monitored' (BLOCKING). If a main highway collapses, the closed backup route reopens automatically. This takes 30-50 seconds in older STP; modern RSTP does it in milliseconds.
encounters.question: A city has three highway interchanges forming a perfect triangle. To prevent drivers from getting stuck in an infinite loop, traffic engineers must block one of the three connecting roads. What is this concept called in networking?
encounters.explanation: STP prevents loops by logically blocking redundant paths while keeping them available for failover, ensuring a single loop-free path exists between any two points.

encounters.title: The Grand Architect of the Great Data Highway
encounters.scenario: You're the architect of the Great Data Highway, with separate cities — Finance City, Marketing Town, Engineering District — each strictly isolated. To connect a building to one specific city, you build an ACCESS ROAD (ACCESS PORT) — a car on it belongs to that city and nothing else. But connecting every city to the central Switch Junction with separate bridges would be wasteful, so you build one 'Interstate Bridge' (TRUNK PORT) that carries traffic from ALL cities at once. To keep cars sorted, the '802.1Q sticker system' tags each car as it enters the bridge — a blue sticker for Finance, red for Marketing — and the far end reads the sticker to route the car correctly. There's also a 'Ghost Lane' (NATIVE VLAN) where cars travel with NO sticker — efficient, but a security risk if an intruder slips into it undetected.
encounters.question: You are setting up a connection for a single desktop computer that only belongs to the HR department. Should you configure this connection as an Access Port or a Trunk Port?
encounters.explanation: An Access Port connects an end-device (like a PC) to a single, specific VLAN, much like a driveway leading to one house.

encounters.question: What is the purpose of a VLAN?
options: Create logical broadcast domains on a single switch
Route traffic between different IP subnets
encounters.explanation: A VLAN (Virtual LAN) creates separate logical broadcast domains on a single physical switch. Devices in different VLANs cannot communicate without a Layer 3 device (router or L3 switch).

encounters.question: What type of switch port carries traffic for multiple VLANs using 802.1Q tags?
encounters.explanation: A trunk port carries traffic for multiple VLANs simultaneously, using 802.1Q tags to identify which VLAN each frame belongs to. Access ports carry traffic for only one VLAN (untagged).

encounters.question: What is the total convergence time for original 802.1D Spanning Tree Protocol?
encounters.explanation: STP (802.1D) takes 30–50 seconds to converge: up to 20 seconds in Blocking (Max Age) + 15 seconds Listening + 15 seconds Learning = 50 sec max. This is why RSTP (802.1w) was developed.

encounters.question: An attacker sends frames with a double 802.1Q tag to jump to a different VLAN. What attack is this?
encounters.explanation: VLAN hopping via double tagging: attacker sends a frame with two 802.1Q tags. The first tag matches the native VLAN (stripped by first switch), and the inner tag reaches VLAN of attacker's choice on the second switch.

encounters.title: The Ghost in the Switch
encounters.scenario:
You enter the 'Switching Sanctum' where the ethereal flow of data is guarded by a spectral entity known as the VLAN-Wraith. The Wraith feeds on misconfigured trunk ports, allowing it to leap across network segments that should be isolated.

The wraith utilizes a technique called 'Double Tagging.' By sending a frame with two 802.1Q tags—the first matching the native VLAN of the first switch and the second being the target destination—it tricks the infrastructure into stripping the outer layer and forwarding it to an unauthorized zone. To banish this ghost, you must ensure that the native VLAN is never set to the default (VLAN 1) and is instead assigned to a dedicated, unused ID.
encounters.question: In a double-tagging attack, how does the first switch process a frame containing two 802.1Q tags?
options: It ignores both tags and drops the packet immediately.
It strips the outer tag (matching the native VLAN) and forwards it to the next switch.
It replaces the inner tag with the outer tag before forwarding.
It encapsulates both tags into a new header for security.
encounters.explanation: The correct answer is B. In double tagging, the first switch strips the outer tag because it matches its native VLAN; the second switch then sees the inner tag and forwards it to the target VLAN. Option A is incorrect because the switch doesn't recognize it as a threat initially. Option C is not how 802.1Q works. Option D describes encapsulation, which is not part of this attack vector.

encounters.title: The Gatekeeper of the Fractured Realms
encounters.scenario:
You stand before the 'Great Partition,' a shimmering wall of logic separating the Merchant District (VLAN 10) from the Archive Vault (VLAN 20). The flow of commerce has ground to a halt because the data-scrolls cannot pass through the gate. The merchants are desperate, and their trade routes are blocked by an invisible barrier.

The Gatekeeper, a towering construct of copper and fiber, hums with static as you approach. 'The bridge is broken,' it booms in a synthesized voice. 'The path for the merchants is carved into the stone, but the vault's entrance remains hidden from the Great Map. Unless you can identify why the gateway is incomplete, the realms shall remain divided.'

You consult your scrolls—the configuration logs of the Layer 3 switch. You see that an SVI (Switch Virtual Interface) has been successfully established for VLAN 10, providing a valid gateway for those users. However, there is no SVI defined for VLAN 20. Because the Layer 3 switch lacks a logical interface to 'touch' the second network, it cannot route traffic between the two distinct subnets.

The Gatekeeper demands you identify the specific technical reason why packets from the Merchant District are being dropped before they can reach the Archive Vault.
encounters.question: A technician reports that hosts in VLAN 10 cannot reach a server in VLAN 20. The Layer 3 switch has an SVI for VLAN 10, but no SVI exists for VLAN 20. What is the primary reason the traffic fails to route?
options: The trunk links between switches are not carrying 802.1Q tagged frames.
The Layer 3 switch cannot route between subnets if it lacks a valid Layer 3 interface (SVI) for one of the participating VLANs.
The default gateway on the host in VLAN 10 is missing its subnet mask.
The Layer 3 switch is not running a dynamic routing protocol like OSPF or EIGRP.
encounters.explanation: In Inter-VLAN routing using SVIs, the SVI acts as the default gateway for the devices in that specific VLAN. For a Layer 3 switch to route traffic between two different VLANs, it must have an active and configured SVI for both VLANs involved. If VLAN 20 lacks an SVI, the switch has no logical interface to 'enter' or 'exit' that network, meaning it cannot move packets from the SVI of VLAN 10 into the domain of VLAN 20.

encounters.title: The Gate of Segmented Realms
encounters.scenario:
You stand before a massive stone gate guarded by a spectral sentinel. The gate is divided into several chambers, each requiring its own unique magical signature to enter. To pass through the main corridor, you must configure the 'Switchport' sigils to ensure only specific travelers can reach specific rooms.

To create a new realm (VLAN), you must use the command 'vlan [ID]'. Once created, you must define the nature of the port connecting to it. For a standard traveler, you apply 'switchport mode access' and assign them to their specific domain with 'switchport access vlan [ID]'. If you need a gateway that allows multiple realms to pass through at once, you must designate it as a trunk using 'switchport mode trunk'.
encounters.question: You need to configure a port on a Cisco switch so that it only carries traffic for VLAN 10. Which sequence of commands is correct?
options: switchport mode trunk, switchport access vlan 10
vlan 10, switchport mode access, switchport access vlan 10
encounters.explanation: To correctly configure an access port for a specific VLAN on a Cisco switch, you must first create the VLAN in global configuration (vlan 10), set the port to access mode (switchport mode access), and then assign that port to the specific VLAN (switchport access vlan 10). 'Switchport mode trunk' is used for ports carrying multiple VLANs.

nodes.name: Airwaves
nodes.description: Wireless standards, security protocols, channel planning, and AP architecture.

encounters.title: The Caffeine Connection: Wireless Chaos
encounters.scenario: You settle into a corner booth at 'The Caffeine Connection' coffee shop, and the wireless air is chaos. The 2.4GHz band is a narrow, one-lane road packed with slow-moving traffic — microwaves, Bluetooth devices, and dozens of phones all fighting for the same space. Switching to 5GHz feels like a high-speed express lane — but signal strength drops sharply the moment you move behind a heavy wooden pillar. A stranger nearby is running a packet-sniffing tool, and the shop's aging router still uses WPA2, leaving it vulnerable to handshake-capture attacks. Navigating this requires understanding how 802.11 standards (from old 802.11n to modern 802.11ax) and encryption (WPA2 vs the much stronger WPA3) interact with frequency to create a stable, secure connection.
encounters.question: You are trying to connect to the Wi-Fi in a crowded cafe. Which frequency is like a wide, multi-lane highway that offers much higher speeds but has a shorter range and struggles with walls?
encounters.explanation: 5GHz provides higher data rates and less congestion (more 'lanes'), but its shorter wavelength means it doesn't penetrate walls and obstacles as well as 2.4GHz.

encounters.title: The Bouncer's Secret Handshake: WPA2 vs WPA3
encounters.scenario: Picture the Wi-Fi password as a secret whispered to a bouncer outside a club. Under WPA2-Personal, every guest whispers the SAME password during a 4-WAY HANDSHAKE — and someone nearby with a packet sniffer can capture that entire exchange without ever entering the club. Taken home, that recording can be brute-forced offline against millions of guesses, with nobody at the club ever knowing — an OFFLINE DICTIONARY ATTACK, WPA2-PSK's biggest weakness against weak passwords. WPA3-Personal fixes this with SAE ('Dragonfly') — both sides cryptographically PROVE they know the password without ever transmitting anything crackable. Even a fully-recorded SAE exchange is useless offline; every guess requires live interaction with the AP, which can detect and lock out repeated failures. WPA3 also enforces PMF, blocking forged deauth frames used to force a fresh handshake.
encounters.question: An attacker sits in a cafe's parking lot and passively records the WPA2-PSK 4-way handshake of the cafe's Wi-Fi as customers connect. They take the capture home to brute-force it overnight. If the cafe instead used WPA3-Personal (SAE), what would change about this attack?
options: Nothing - SAE uses the same handshake as WPA2 and is equally vulnerable to offline cracking
The captured exchange would be useless for offline guessing - each password attempt requires live interaction with the AP, which can detect and throttle repeated failures
SAE eliminates the need for a password entirely, so there is nothing to capture
SAE only protects enterprise networks with a RADIUS server, so a personal/PSK cafe network gains no benefit
encounters.explanation: SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) is a Diffie-Hellman-based exchange — a passively captured SAE exchange gives an attacker nothing to brute-force offline, since every guess needs a live round-trip the AP can rate-limit or lock out. Wrong: (A) this offline-cracking weakness is exactly what SAE fixes versus WPA2's 4-way handshake. (C) WPA3-Personal still uses a passphrase; SAE just changes how it's verified. (D) SAE replaces PSK in WPA3-Personal (no RADIUS needed) — WPA3-Enterprise is a separate mode.

encounters.question: Which 802.11 standard operates exclusively on the 5 GHz band with a maximum theoretical speed of 3.5 Gbps?
encounters.explanation: 802.11ac (Wi-Fi 5) operates exclusively on 5 GHz and achieves up to 3.5 Gbps using MU-MIMO and 80/160 MHz channel bonding. 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6) supports 2.4/5/6 GHz.

encounters.question: On the 2.4 GHz band, which three channels are non-overlapping?
encounters.explanation: Channels 1, 6, and 11 are the only non-overlapping channels in the 2.4 GHz band (in North America). Using any other combination results in co-channel or adjacent-channel interference.

encounters.question: WPA3 replaces WPA2's PSK with which authentication method that prevents offline dictionary attacks?
encounters.explanation: WPA3 Personal uses SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) — a key exchange method that prevents offline dictionary attacks. Even if an attacker captures the 4-way handshake, they cannot crack the password offline.

encounters.title: The Spectrum Sieve
encounters.scenario:
You stand before the Great Antennae of the Wireless Plains. To pass, you must prove your knowledge of the ancient Wi-Fi scrolls (802.11 standards). The air is thick with signals, and you must distinguish between the frequencies used by different generations of technology.

You recall that 802.11a operates on 5 GHz, while 802.11b/g/n primarily inhabit the 2.4 GHz band. Modern standards like 802.11ac are strictly 5 GHz (with Wave 2 capable of high speeds), whereas 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6) and 802.11be (Wi-Fi 7) are versatile, operating on both 2.4 and 5 GHz, with the latter even reaching into the 6 GHz realm.
encounters.question: Which of the following Wi-Fi standards operates on both the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands?
encounters.explanation: The correct answer is B (802.11ax). 802.11ac is only 5 GHz; 802.11b is only 2.4 GHz; 802.11a is only 5 GHz. 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6) and 802.11be are the modern standards that support both common bands.

encounters.title: The Echoing Woods
encounters.scenario:
You enter a dense thicket where the 'Whispers of Interference' make communication difficult. The trees are crowded with signals overlapping in the 2.4 GHz frequency space, causing packets to collide and vanish into the void.

To navigate safely, you must identify the clear paths. In North America, the 2.4 GHz band is divided such that only three specific channels do not overlap with their neighbors. Using adjacent channels, like 1 and 2 or 5 and 6, causes significant interference because the signals bleed into one another.
encounters.question: Which set of channels provides non-overlapping coverage in the 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi band?
encounters.explanation: The correct answer is C. Channels 1, 6, and 11 are the standard non-overlapping channels in the 2.4 GHz band. Other combinations (like 1, 5, 9) result in overlapping signals that cause interference.

encounters.title: The Spectral Static of the Overlapping Realms
encounters.scenario:
You enter the 'Valley of Whispers,' where the very air vibrates with a discordant hum. A spectral guardian named Aether-Glitch manifests before you, its form flickering like a dying signal. It feeds on the chaotic overlap of waves, growing more powerful as nearby magical beacons bleed into one another's frequencies.

The guardian shrieks, 'Many voices scream in the same space! They collide and blur, creating a cacophony that weakens the weave!' You notice three distinct towers pulsing with light; however, their signals are bleeding together, causing massive packet loss for your party's communication spells. 
To banish the entity, you must realign the magical beacons to a configuration that ensures clear, non-overlapping paths. If you fail to identify the correct frequency spacing, the interference will overwhelm your senses, and the guardian will feast on your connection.
encounters.question: The spectral guardian demands you stabilize the local weave. To eliminate co-channel and adjacent-channel interference in the 2.4 GHz band, which set of channels should be utilized for the beacon towers?
encounters.explanation: In the 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi band, each channel is approximately 20 MHz wide, but they are spaced only 5 MHz apart. This means that many channels overlap with their neighbors (adjacent-channel interference). To provide clear, non-overlapping paths for signals, the industry standard is to use channels 1, 6, and 11. Using other combinations like 1, 4, or 7 causes signal bleed, which creates noise and degrades performance for all devices in the vicinity.

encounters.title: Whispers in the Aether
encounters.scenario:
The air hums with invisible frequencies as you enter the Echo Chamber. To navigate the maze, you must distinguish between the different layers of wireless signals floating through the air.

Every signal has a name that humans can see and interact with; this is the SSID (Service Set Identifier). However, underneath that lies the BSSID, which is the unique MAC address of the specific Access Point or radio hardware. In larger realms where multiple towers broadcast the same human-readable name to create one seamless network, that shared logical identity is known as an ESSID.
encounters.question: A technician identifies a wireless signal and notes its unique MAC address. Which term describes this specific identifier?
encounters.explanation: The BSSID is the unique MAC address of the specific Access Point or radio. The SSID is the human-readable name (e.g., 'Guest_WiFi'), and the ESSID is the logical name that can span multiple APs.

encounters.title: The Scout's Survey
encounters.scenario:
You are tasked with establishing a communication link across the Great Wasteland. You must choose the correct magical focus (antenna) to ensure your signals reach their destination without being lost in the void.

Omnidirectional antennas are used when you need 360-degree coverage for local areas, while directional, patch, or Yagi antennas are required to focus a signal toward a specific point. Before building anything, you must perform a site survey—a critical ritual to identify dead zones, potential interference from other magic, and the optimal placement of your relay towers.
encounters.question: Which antenna type would be most appropriate for a point-to-point link between two distant towers?
encounters.explanation: Directional antennas (including patch and Yagi) focus the signal in a specific direction, making them ideal for point-to-point links. Omnidirectional antennas radiate in all directions and are better for general local coverage.

nodes.name: Physical Foundations
nodes.description: Data center infrastructure, MDF/IDF, UPS types, and environmental considerations.

encounters.title: The Data Highway Project
encounters.scenario: You're the Chief Infrastructure Engineer laying copper pipelines for high-speed data across a digital valley. First, choose your pipe grade: some are narrow and prone to interference from nearby heavy machinery (UTP), others are heavily armored against electromagnetic noise (STP). For tier, Cat5e is the old country road — reliable but limited speed. Cat6 is a modern highway — faster, but needs tighter construction to avoid signal bleed. Cat6a is the super-highway — massive throughput over longer distances. One unbreakable law: SIGNAL DECAY — stretch a pipeline too far without a repeater and the flow becomes sluggish and unreliable. And every junction must follow the TIA-568 wiring standard — mismatched wiring patterns cause traffic to crash at every intersection.
encounters.question: You are laying a pipeline next to a massive, vibrating power plant that generates heavy electromagnetic noise. Which type of cabling should you use?
encounters.explanation: STP includes shielding to protect the signal from EMI (Electromagnetic Interference), much like an armored pipe protects fluid from external pressure or contaminants.

encounters.title: The Corporate Org Chart: MDF and IDF Wiring Hierarchy
encounters.scenario: Picture a company's mail system across a 10-story tower. All outside mail arrives at one central mailroom in the lobby — the MDF (Main Distribution Frame): core switches, routers, the ISP demarc, and main patch panels live here. From there, big bundles travel up to each floor via pneumatic tube — your BACKBONE (vertical) cabling, almost always fiber, since a single copper run from lobby to 10th floor would be far too long. Each floor has its own small mailroom — the IDF (Intermediate Distribution Frame) — whose clerk (an access-layer switch) sorts the bundle into individual office runs. That walk from IDF to office door is HORIZONTAL CABLING, capped by TIA-568 at 90m permanent link / 100m total channel. Key insight: ONE MDF per building, ONE IDF per floor/wing, fed by backbone cabling and feeding end devices via horizontal cabling.
encounters.question: A new office is being fitted out on the 8th floor of a building whose MDF is in the basement. The office desk is 70 meters of cable away from the 8th floor's IDF, but the IDF itself is connected to the basement MDF via a 200-meter fiber backbone run. Is this a valid design?
options: No - the desk's 70m run plus the 200m backbone exceeds the 100m TIA-568 limit, so the whole path is non-compliant
Yes - the 90m/100m TIA-568 horizontal cabling limit applies only to the IDF-to-desk run (70m, which is fine); the IDF-to-MDF backbone uses fiber, which is not bound by the 100m copper limit
No - IDFs are not allowed to connect to desks directly, only to the MDF
Yes, but only if the backbone cabling is also copper to keep latency consistent
encounters.explanation: The 90m/100m TIA-568 limit applies to HORIZONTAL copper cabling — the IDF-to-desk run, here 70m, well within budget. Backbone (vertical) cabling between IDF and MDF is typically fiber precisely because it often spans much further than 100m, with distance limits measured in kilometers. Wrong: (A) incorrectly adds the two runs as one copper segment. (C) connecting end devices is the IDF's entire purpose. (D) is backwards — fiber is preferred for long backbone runs specifically because it ISN'T limited like copper.

encounters.question: What does MDF stand for in network infrastructure?
encounters.explanation: MDF (Main Distribution Frame) is the central wiring point for a building's network — housing core switches, routers, WAN connections, and patch panels. All IDFs connect back to the MDF.

encounters.question: What type of UPS has zero transfer time because it always routes power through the inverter?
encounters.explanation: Online/double conversion UPS always runs through the inverter — utility power charges the battery, and the inverter powers the load 100% of the time. Zero transfer time on outage, cleanest power output.

encounters.question: What is the maximum horizontal cable run length (permanent link) defined by TIA-568?
encounters.explanation: TIA-568 specifies maximum 90m for the permanent horizontal link (wall jack to patch panel). Up to 10m is allowed for patch cables (both ends), giving a total of 100m channel length.

encounters.title: The Power Vault
encounters.scenario:
Deep within the core of the fortress, you find the Mainframe. It is powered by a flickering energy source. A storm is approaching, and you must choose the correct Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) to protect the servers from surges and outages.

You analyze three types: Offline/Standby UPS, which only kicks in when power fails; Line-interactive, which monitors the line and switches to battery if conditions degrade; and Online/Double-conversion, which is the gold standard. The latter constantly converts power through an inverter, ensuring the load never sees a flicker or a spike from the raw grid.
encounters.question: Which UPS topology provides the highest level of protection by continuously running the load through an inverter?
encounters.explanation: The correct answer is C. Online/Double-conversion UPS systems provide the best protection because they constantly convert AC to DC and back to AC, isolating the equipment from power fluctuations. Offline and Line-interactive models have a brief delay when switching to battery.

encounters.title: The Warden of the Eternal Current
encounters.scenario:
You stand before the Great Vault of the Core, where the primary servers pulse with a rhythmic blue light. The air hums with static electricity as a spectral figure—the Warden of the Grid—manifests from the humming cabinets. 'Many seekers enter this chamber,' the Warden booms, 'but few can maintain the flow. The grid is treacherous; it flickers like a dying candle. To protect the Core, you must choose the ultimate shield against the instability of the world outside.'

The Warden points toward three different power stabilization arrays. One reacts only when the lights fail; another adjusts for voltage swings but takes a fraction of a second to switch sources. The third, however, maintains a constant cycle, feeding the servers through a continuous conversion process that isolates them from every tremor in the electrical line.

The Warden's eyes glow with intensity as he poses his final riddle: 'If the Core must never falter—not for a millisecond, not even during a minor sag—which architecture provides the absolute sanctuary of constant isolation?'
encounters.question: Which UPS topology is required to ensure that mission-critical servers are completely isolated from power fluctuations and experience zero transfer time during a voltage sag?
encounters.explanation: Standby (Offline) UPS systems only engage once power is lost, which can cause a reboot during the switchover. Line-Interactive systems use a transformer or regulator to handle minor sags but still have a brief delay when switching to battery. Double-conversion (Online) units constantly convert AC to DC and back to AC. This creates a continuous buffer, ensuring that the equipment is always running on 'clean' power from an inverter, making it the only choice for mission-critical systems where even a millisecond of interruption is unacceptable.

encounters.title: The Forge of Power Distribution
encounters.scenario:
You enter the subterranean power vault where the realm's infrastructure is housed in massive metal racks. To keep the machines running, you must manage the distribution of energy and the physical space they occupy.

Standard PDUs provide basic power, but 'Switched' PDUs allow you to toggle individual outlets remotely, while 'Metered' PDUs track how much power each device consumes. Every piece of equipment takes up a specific amount of vertical space; 1U is equal to 1.75 inches. You must also guard against the primary enemy: high temperatures, which can fry the circuits if airflow and humidity are not monitored.
encounters.question: A technician needs to monitor the power consumption of several servers in a rack. Which type of PDU should they install?
encounters.explanation: A Metered PDU is specifically designed to show the current draw (power consumption) of the connected devices. A Switched PDU allows for remote control of outlets, and a Basic PDU provides only standard power distribution.

nodes.name: The Power Standard
nodes.description: Power over Ethernet standards, power negotiation, and cable considerations for PoE deployments.

encounters.title: The Ether-Grid Engineer
encounters.scenario: You're managing the 'Ether-Grid,' where data and electricity share the same conduits via Power over Ethernet (PoE). Your PoE switch is the central power plant with a finite POWER BUDGET — plug in too many high-draw devices without checking total wattage, and the grid suffers a brownout, leaving devices unpowered. Service tiers: 802.3af is a small residential transformer — just enough for basic VoIP phones. 802.3at (PoE+) is an industrial-grade line for medium devices like PTZ cameras. 802.3bt (PoE++) is the high-capacity grid for heavy equipment. For wiring: 'Mode A' delivers power over the data-carrying wires (like cars and fuel trucks sharing lanes), while 'Mode B' uses separate dedicated lines for power.
encounters.question: You are setting up a small office with basic VoIP phones that require very little power. Which 'grid standard' is the bare minimum required?
encounters.explanation: 802.3af is the original PoE standard, providing up to 15.4W — sufficient for low-power devices like basic VoIP phones.

encounters.title: The Power Plant Manager: Budgeting the Grid
encounters.scenario: As Power Plant Manager, your PoE switch has a fixed POWER BUDGET — say 400W total across 24 ports. Each connected device requests a service tier: a basic VoIP phone (802.3af, up to 15.4W) is residential service. A PTZ camera or Wi-Fi 6 AP (802.3at/PoE+, up to 30W) is commercial service — roughly double. The newest 802.3bt (PoE++) devices can request up to 60W (Type 3) or 90W (Type 4) — industrial service. You can never promise more total power than the plant generates: if 350W of your 400W is already reserved and a new 90W device connects, the switch simply can't power that port. Always add up each device's CLASS-based draw against the total budget before deploying, leaving headroom for growth.
encounters.question: A 24-port switch advertises a 400W PoE power budget. The network team plans to deploy 10 Wi-Fi 6 access points, each negotiating as 802.3at (PoE+) Class 4 devices drawing 25.5W each. After installing all 10 APs, how much of the power budget remains, and is the deployment safe?
options: 255W consumed, 145W remaining - safe, with headroom for a few more low-power devices like phones
400W consumed exactly - safe, but with zero headroom for any future devices
255W consumed, but unsafe because PoE+ devices require the switch to reserve double their rated class power
510W consumed - unsafe, exceeds the 400W budget by 110W
encounters.explanation: 10 APs x 25.5W = 255W. 400W - 255W = 145W remaining — plenty of headroom for a few more low-power devices like phones (15.4W each) later. Wrong: (B) miscounts the total as exactly 400W. (C) invents a 'double reservation' rule that doesn't exist — the switch reserves the negotiated class wattage, not double. (D) doubles the AP power draw incorrectly (10 x 51W instead of 10 x 25.5W). Always do this math BEFORE a rollout.

encounters.question: Which IEEE standard provides 15.4W of power per port?
encounters.explanation: 802.3af (Type 1) delivers 15.4W max, with 12.95W available to the device after cable loss.

encounters.question: Your VoIP phone needs 25W. Which PoE standard is the minimum required?
encounters.explanation: 802.3at (Type 2 / PoE+) provides up to 30W, supporting devices like PTZ cameras and VoIP phones.

encounters.question: 48-port switch with 740W budget. 20 APs (25W each) + 15 cameras (15W each). Enough power?
encounters.explanation: 20 APs × 25 W = 500 W. 15 cameras × 15 W = 225 W. Total draw = 725 W. With a 740 W budget, 740 - 725 = 15 W remains. The switch has enough power for this deployment.

encounters.title: The Warden of the Overloaded Grid
encounters.scenario:
The air in the Command Center is thick with the smell of ozone and melting plastic. Before you stands a towering spectral entity composed of tangled copper wiring and crackling electricity—the Static Wraith. It guards the primary distribution switch, its form flickering as it feeds on the unstable power fluctuations of the failing network.

To bypass the Warden, you must stabilize the local area network by correctly configuring the Power over Ethernet (PoE) parameters. The fortress's defense system relies on 12 Access Points (APs) to maintain a secure perimeter. If the switch cannot provide enough guaranteed power to these devices, the signal will collapse, and the Wraith will consume your connection.

You access the terminal and see the hardware specifications: The switch has a total PoE power budget of 370W. While each AP actually draws 25W of power during peak operation, the current infrastructure only supports the IEEE 802.3af standard. You must determine if the configuration is viable based on the guaranteed limits provided by that specific standard.
encounters.question: Based on the technical specifications provided, does the switch have enough power to support all 12 Access Points using the per-port guarantee of the 802.3af standard?
options: Yes, because the total guaranteed power (12 APs × 15.4W) is 184.8W, which falls well within the 370W budget.
No, because the actual draw of 25W per AP exceeds the 15.4W limit of the 802.3af standard.
Yes, because the total actual power consumption (12 APs × 25W) is 300W, which is under the 370W budget.
No, because a switch with a 370W budget can only support up to 14 devices regardless of the standard.
encounters.explanation: The correct answer is A. In PoE calculations, when a specific standard like 802.3af is specified, you must calculate based on that standard's guaranteed power per port. Since 12 APs × 15.4W (the 802.3af guarantee) equals 184.8W, and the switch has a total budget of 370W, the requirement is met. While the actual draw is higher (300W), the question specifically asks about the calculation based on the per-port guarantee. Note: In real-world scenarios, if an AP requires 25W but only receives 15.4W from an 802.3af port, it may fail to boot; however, for this specific logic check, the guarantee is the deciding factor.

encounters.title: The Totems of Eternal Light
encounters.scenario:
You find a series of ancient totems that need to be powered by the realm's grid. However, not all totems draw the same amount of energy; some are small lanterns, while others are massive beacons.

You must choose the correct Power over Ethernet (PoE) standard for each. 802.3af (Type 1) provides up to 15.4W—enough for simple devices. 802.3at (Type 2, or PoE+) provides up to 30W for more demanding equipment. For the most powerful artifacts requiring 60W or even 100W, you must use the 802.3bt (Type 3/4) standard.
encounters.question: Which PoE standard is required to power a high-demand device that requires up to 30 Watts of power?
encounters.explanation: 802.3at (Type 2, also known as PoE+) provides up to 30W of power. 802.3af only provides up to 15.4W, and 802.3bt is required for even higher demands (60W+).

guardian_encounters.question: Which routing protocol is used between Autonomous Systems on the internet?
guardian_encounters.explanation: BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) is the EGP (Exterior Gateway Protocol) that routes between ASes on the internet. OSPF, EIGRP, and RIP are IGPs used within a single AS.

guardian_encounters.question: OSPF has an administrative distance of:
guardian_encounters.explanation: OSPF = AD 110. The AD pecking order: Connected(0) > Static(1) > eBGP(20) > EIGRP(90) > OSPF(110) > RIP(120) > iBGP(200).

guardian_encounters.question: An attacker sends frames tagged with the native VLAN ID followed by an inner tag for VLAN 20. What attack is this, and what is the primary mitigation?
options: ARP poisoning — mitigated by dynamic ARP inspection
VLAN hopping (double tagging) — mitigated by changing native VLAN to an unused VLAN
STP manipulation — mitigated by BPDU Guard
MAC flooding — mitigated by port security
guardian_encounters.explanation: Double tagging VLAN hopping: attacker's frame has outer tag = native VLAN (stripped by first switch) and inner tag = target VLAN (delivered by second switch). Mitigation: change native VLAN to an unused VLAN (not VLAN 1) and disable DTP.

guardian_encounters.title: The Gate of Prefix Logic
guardian_encounters.scenario: A spectral sentinel blocks the path to the core switch. It demands you resolve a conflict in the routing table: two paths exist for the same destination.
guardian_encounters.question: A router learns 192.168.0.0/16 via EIGRP (AD 90) and 192.168.1.0/24 via OSPF (AD 110). Which route is installed in the routing table?
options: Neither, as OSPF has a higher AD
guardian_encounters.explanation: The Longest Prefix Match rule takes precedence over Administrative Distance. Because /24 is a more specific subnet than /16, the router will select the OSPF route regardless of its higher AD.

guardian_encounters.title: The Weaver's Subinterface
guardian_encounters.scenario: A weaver of threads stands before a single physical cable that must carry the voices of many different kingdoms (VLANs).
guardian_encounters.question: What is the primary purpose of configuring subinterfaces on a router?
options: To increase the physical clock speed of the port
To allow a single physical interface to route traffic for multiple VLANs
To provide hardware-level redundancy for failed ports
To encrypt data passing between different local segments
guardian_encounters.explanation: Subinterfaces (often used in 'Router-on-a-Stick' configurations) allow a single physical interface to be divided into multiple logical interfaces, each assigned to a different VLAN.

guardian_encounters.title: The Spirit of Cost
guardian_encounters.scenario: A spirit of the winds demands to know which path is calculated by the weight of its speed.
guardian_encounters.question: Which routing protocol uses 'cost' as a metric based primarily on link bandwidth?
guardian_encounters.explanation: OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) uses 'cost' as its metric, which is calculated based on the bandwidth of the outgoing interface.

guardian_encounters.title: The Twin Gate Guardians
guardian_encounters.scenario: Two identical golems stand side-by-side. They share a single identity to provide a seamless gateway for the travelers.
guardian_encounters.question: In an HSRP configuration, what is the term for the IP address shared by the active and standby routers?
guardian_encounters.explanation: HSRP (Hot Standby Router Protocol) provides redundancy by having multiple routers share a Virtual IP (VIP) and a virtual MAC address.

guardian_encounters.title: The Shadow Path
guardian_encounters.scenario: A hidden path lies in the shadows; it only reveals itself when the main road is blocked by falling debris.
guardian_encounters.question: A floating static route is configured with an Administrative Distance (AD) of 200. When does this route become active?
options: When the physical link to the primary router fails
When the primary route's AD is manually increased
When the primary route with a lower AD is removed from the routing table
When the router receives an OSPF update for that prefix
guardian_encounters.explanation: A floating static route has a higher Administrative Distance than the primary route. It remains 'hidden' in the configuration until the primary (lower AD) route is removed from the routing table.

guardian_encounters.title: The Gatekeeper of Segments
guardian_encounters.scenario: A spectral wall blocks your path to the inner sanctum. To pass, you must prove your mastery over logical separation.
guardian_encounters.question: To carve a new VLAN into the fabric of the network on a Cisco switch, which mode must you enter?
guardian_encounters.explanation: To create or modify a VLAN (e.g., 'switch(config-vlan)#'), you must be in Global Configuration mode. Interface Configuration mode is used for assigning ports to existing VLANs.

guardian_encounters.title: The Nexus Sentinel
guardian_encounters.scenario: A floating stone monolith hums with energy. It demands to know how a Layer 3 switch bridges the gap between segments.
guardian_encounters.question: What is the primary purpose of an SVI (Switched Virtual Interface) on a Layer 3 switch?
options: To provide a physical port for end-user devices
To provide a routed gateway interface for a VLAN
To map MAC addresses to specific IP addresses
To broadcast traffic across all available subnets
guardian_encounters.explanation: An SVI is a logical interface (like Interface Vlan 10) that allows a Layer 3 switch to route traffic between different VLANs by acting as the default gateway.

guardian_encounters.title: The Weaver of Bonds
guardian_encounters.scenario: A spider-like construct weaves multiple physical links into one logical path. It demands the name of the ancient standard.
guardian_encounters.question: Which IEEE standard is specifically used for link aggregation and EtherChannel with LACP?
guardian_encounters.explanation: IEEE 802.3ad is the standard for Link Aggregation (LAG), which allows multiple physical links to be combined into a single logical link for increased bandwidth and redundancy.

guardian_encounters.title: The Voice of the Echo
guardian_encounters.scenario: A ghostly voice echoes through the halls. To silence it, you must isolate the communication frequencies from the data stream.
guardian_encounters.question: When connecting an IP phone to a switch port, which feature is used to separate voice traffic from data traffic?
guardian_encounters.explanation: A Voice VLAN allows a switch to identify and prioritize voice traffic (VoIP) over data traffic, often using a different subnet or priority level for the phone's traffic.

guardian_encounters.title: The Frame Watcher
guardian_encounters.scenario: A mechanical eye tracks every frame passing through the switch. It demands to know how it remembers where they came from.
guardian_encounters.question: What specific information does a switch examine to build its MAC address table?
options: Source MAC address of incoming frames
guardian_encounters.explanation: A switch builds its MAC address table by looking at the source MAC address of an incoming frame. This allows it to know which port a specific device is connected to.

guardian_encounters.title: The Spectral Sentinel
guardian_encounters.scenario: A shimmering barrier of high-frequency waves blocks the path. A spectral guardian demands you identify the correct standard to pass through the 5 GHz gate.
guardian_encounters.question: Which 802.11 standard operates exclusively in the 5 GHz band and is also known as Wi-Fi 5?
guardian_encounters.explanation: 802.11ac (Wi-Fi 5) operates exclusively in the 5 GHz band. While 802.11n can operate on both 2.4 and 5 GHz, and 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6) is the successor to ac.

guardian_encounters.title: The Beacon of Identity
guardian_encounters.scenario: A floating sigil flickers in the air with several names. To pass, you must identify the specific term for a wireless network's broadcast name.
guardian_encounters.question: What is the broadcast name of a wireless network called?
guardian_encounters.explanation: SSID (Service Set Identifier) is the unique name assigned to a wireless network for identification by users.

guardian_encounters.title: The Radiating Aegis
guardian_encounters.scenario: A guardian stands atop a tower, its energy radiating in all directions to cover the valley. You must identify the antenna type that provides this 360-degree coverage.
guardian_encounters.question: Which antenna type radiates signal in all directions?
guardian_encounters.explanation: An omnidirectional antenna radiates signals in all directions (360 degrees), making it ideal for general coverage areas.

guardian_encounters.title: The Peerless Pact
guardian_encounters.scenario: Two rogue spirits are communicating directly with each other without a central hub or tower. They demand you name the mode that allows direct peer-to-peer connections.
guardian_encounters.question: Which wireless network mode involves devices connecting directly to each other without an Access Point (AP)?
guardian_encounters.explanation: Ad-hoc mode (Independent Basic Service Set or IBSS) allows devices to communicate directly with each other without the need for a central Access Point.

guardian_encounters.title: The Void of Silence
guardian_encounters.scenario: You enter a cavern where the signal drops to zero and your HUD flickers red. A guardian mocks you for entering an area with no coverage.
guardian_encounters.question: In a wireless site survey, what is the term for an area where the signal is too weak for reliable communication?
guardian_encounters.explanation: A dead zone (or coverage hole) is an area where the wireless signal is too weak to maintain a reliable connection due to distance or physical obstructions.

guardian_encounters.title: The Remote Sentinel
guardian_encounters.scenario: A remote outpost's server has frozen due to a logic loop. You cannot travel there physically to perform a manual reboot.
guardian_encounters.question: What specific capability does a switched PDU provide to an administrator in this situation?
guardian_encounters.explanation: A Switched Power Distribution Unit (PDU) allows administrators to remotely control and power cycle individual outlets, enabling the rebooting of equipment in remote locations without physical access.

guardian_encounters.title: The Heat of the Forge
guardian_encounters.scenario: The server room's cooling fans are whining as the ambient temperature rises. The Guardian warns that heat is the primary enemy of silicon.
guardian_encounters.question: Which environmental factor is most likely to cause hardware failure in a server room?
guardian_encounters.explanation: While dust and humidity are concerns, overheating/high temperature is the most immediate and common environmental factor leading to hardware failure in server environments.

guardian_encounters.title: The Architect's Measure
guardian_encounters.scenario: You are organizing the server racks in the central hub. You need to calculate how much vertical space each device will occupy.
guardian_encounters.question: What is the standard unit of measurement for rack-mounted equipment height?
guardian_encounters.explanation: The 'U' (or Rack Unit) is the standard unit of measurement for the height of equipment in a rack, where 1U equals 1.75 inches.

guardian_encounters.title: The Power Conduit
guardian_encounters.scenario: You need to power a high-performance security camera at the gate. It requires more juice than standard PoE can provide.
guardian_encounters.question: Which PoE standard is capable of providing up to 30W per port?
guardian_encounters.explanation: The IEEE 802.3at standard, also known as PoE+, can provide up to 30W of power per port, making it suitable for devices like PTZ cameras or high-power VOIP phones.

guardian_encounters.title: The Copper Path
guardian_encounters.scenario: You are laying down the copper backbone through the tunnels. You must ensure the signal remains strong enough to reach the next hub.
guardian_encounters.question: What is the maximum cable distance for Ethernet runs per the TIA/EIA-568 standard?
guardian_encounters.explanation: The TIA/EIA-568 standard specifies a maximum length of 100 meters (328 feet) for Ethernet runs to ensure signal integrity and prevent degradation.
